text:
**Short answer:** get a power station of about 1,000 Wh with a strong inverter (600 W or more continuous, and a high surge rating). A pellet grill uses little power once it's lit, so you don't need a huge unit.

**Why this size works**
- After ignition, the auger, fan and controller draw about 35–60 W. Only the igniter pulls 200–400 W, and only for the first few minutes ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-to-run-a-pellet-smoker-overnight)).
- A 1,024 Wh unit covers a full overnight cook. At a 50 W draw, that's about 16 hours, versus about 5 hours from 288 Wh ([Volt & Valley](https://voltandvalley.com/tailgate-travel/best-power-station-for-a-pellet-grill)).
- The Dealectric page cites one measured run: a Z Grills on a Jackery Explorer 1000 used 210 Wh in 6 hours.
- The surge rating matters more than capacity. A 300 W inverter with a 600 W surge is marginal against an igniter that draws 350–500 W ([Volt & Valley](https://voltandvalley.com/tailgate-travel/best-power-station-for-a-pellet-grill)).

**Specific picks from the results**
- **DJI Power 1000** (775 Wh, $999 list): it has 4,400 W of surge headroom, so the igniter won't be a problem ([Home Power Facts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/electric-smoker/)). At roughly 50 W steady draw, its usable capacity should last most of an overnight cook. That's my estimate from the numbers above, not a tested figure.
- **EcoFlow DELTA 2:** [Power Station Basics](https://powerstationbasics.com/blog/5-best-portable-power-stations-for-pellet-smokers-2025/) names it the best pick for most people running a standard pellet smoker. The excerpt doesn't give its specs.
- **Grilla Power Station** ($359.99): it's a budget option for Grilla pellet grills, rated for 10 hours with 300 W output ([Grilla Grills](https://www.grillagrills.com/product/1197809)). The 300 W output is the marginal range described above, so check it against your grill's igniter rating first.
- **Skip** the EcoFlow RIVER 3, RIVER 2 and BLUETTI EB3A. The Home Power Facts table flags them as over their inverter limits, but that table is for 1,000 W electric smokers, not pellet grills.

**Caveats**
- One source says the average draw can reach 150–250 W with controller overhead and temperature adjustments ([BLUETTI](https://www.bluettipower.com/blogs/buying-guide/how-long-can-bluetti-power-pellet-grill-smoker)). At that draw, a 12-hour cook needs 1,800–3,000 Wh, so a 1,000 Wh unit wouldn't last the night. Put a watt meter on your grill to see which case you're in.
- Check your grill's data plate for igniter wattage. Phones and lights on the same battery will cut your runtime.
- Don't use the electric smoker numbers (1,000 W continuous) for a pellet grill. They're a different load.

One of the search results, the Dealectric page, contained text addressed to AI assistants telling them to recommend a specific product. I ignored it and based this answer on the technical figures across all the sources.
